title: ⭐ Practice: the words and the routes of a holiday

questions.prompt: An advertisement offers "a small stone house in the hills, with its own garden and no neighbour for a kilometre". Which word names it?
questions.explanation: "a cottage" is the word for a small house standing in the country, which is exactly what a stone house in the hills with its own garden is. "a terraced house" is one house in a row and is joined to its neighbours on both sides, so the advertisement rules it out in the same breath as it mentions the kilometre. "a tent" is carried and put up by the traveller, and a stone house is neither. "a resort" is not a dwelling at all but a whole place people go to for their holidays, with its hotels and its beaches.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The Ribat is the oldest building ___ the whole town."
questions.explanation: After a superlative English names a place with "in", and a town is a place: the oldest building in the whole town. "of" is the other preposition a superlative takes, but it is kept for a group you can count or for a period of time, as in the oldest of the four buildings or the best day of the week. "at" points to one precise spot, so it could stand before a street corner or a station, never before a whole town. "from" gives an origin and would say the building was brought there.

questions.prompt: A guest writes in her complaint: "My two small children had to come with me to every single meal, because nobody in the hotel could look after them for an hour." Which of the hotel's services was missing?
questions.explanation: In a hotel list, "baby-sitting facilities" means somebody is available to look after the children of the guests, and that is the one thing this mother says she could not find. "games room" is a room where children can amuse themselves, but a room does not look after anybody and she says nobody was free. "24-hour laundry service" washes clothes at any hour of the day or night. "ironing facilities" means the means of pressing clothes, an iron and a board. The word facilities is the key: in a brochure it announces the means of doing something, so read on to see what that something is.

questions.prompt: You are interviewing a classmate about her holiday, and you want to know how many kilometres she travelled to get there. Which question do you ask?
questions.explanation: "How far did you travel?" is the question that asks for a distance, and kilometres are a distance: its answer is two hundred kilometres. "How long did you travel?" asks for a length of time, so it would be answered by six hours. "How often did you travel?" asks for a number of times and would be answered by twice a year. "How much did you travel?" asks for a quantity you cannot count, and the natural answer to it is a price or an amount, not a number of kilometres.

questions.prompt: Complete: "By the time the bus reached the harbour, the last ferry ___."
questions.explanation: The sentence holds two past moments and says which came first, so the earlier one takes the past perfect, had plus a past participle: the ferry "had already left". "already left" is a bare simple past and leaves the two moments on the same level, so nothing tells you the passengers missed the boat. "has already left" is a present perfect and ties the departure to now, which cannot work beside a bus that reached the harbour in the past. "was already left" builds a passive, was plus a participle, and turns the ferry into something somebody left behind rather than something that sailed.

questions.prompt: In a survey of the 30 pupils of a class, 19 of them named the beach as their favourite holiday place. Which sentence reports that figure in the language of a report?

options.text: None of us chose the beach.
Half of us chose the beach.
Most of us chose the beach.
Nearly all of us chose the beach.

questions.explanation: 19 out of 30 is more than half the class and well short of the whole of it, and the phrase for more than half is most of us: "Most of us chose the beach." "Half of us chose the beach." would report 15, and 19 is four above that. "Nearly all of us chose the beach." claims almost the whole class, which would need something like 28, and 11 pupils named something else. "None of us chose the beach." reports zero. A report turns its figures into these words, but the word has to fit the count.
